title: Marguerite and the Hymn
premise: Folklorist Lena Delacroix returns to the village of Hallowmere to record 'The Hymn of Marguerite,' a song locals will sing only once, never twice, and never to completion. As the mirrors in her rented house begin lagging a second behind reality, Lena realizes the song is a binding: its final verse, sung in full, keeps something buried beneath the churchyard asleep—and the last woman who knew it died twelve years ago, on the night Lena first fled. To survive, Lena must learn the verse from Marguerite's ghost without ever singing along, while uncovering that the village's founders drowned an innocent woman and built their peace on her silenced voice. In the end, Lena chooses justice over safety: she sings the true final verse aloud, freeing Marguerite and dooming herself to take her place—until the villagers, shamed into loyalty to truth rather than tradition, join the song and break the cycle.
about_author: August Vane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing hymnals in rural parish libraries before turning to fiction. They write horror about songs, debts, and the things communities agree not to remember.

chapters.title: The House That Listens
chapters.summary: Lena Delacroix arrives in Hallowmere after twelve years away, renting the cottage she once fled. POV: Lena. She unpacks recording equipment and notices the house is unnaturally quiet at dusk—as if holding its breath. The emotional beat is uneasy homecoming: relief at returning tangled with dread she can't name.

chapters.title: A Song Sung Once
chapters.summary: At the village pub, elderly Tom Bracken agrees to sing the folk hymn for Lena's recorder—but stops abruptly before the final verse, pale and shaking. POV: Lena. Locals go silent when she asks why no one sings it twice. Emotional beat: first crack in the village's polite facade; Lena's professional curiosity sharpens into obsession.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Lena wakes to find every mirror in the house reflecting the room one second late: her reflection raises a hand after she does. POV: Lena. She tests it for hours, telling herself it's exhaustion or trickery. Emotional beat: rational denial warring with primal fear—the moment the story becomes horror.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Grave
chapters.summary: In the overgrown corner of the churchyard, Lena finds an unmarked stone and, scratched beneath the moss, the name MARGUERITE. POV: Lena, with a flashback fragment to twelve years earlier. The vicar, Mr. Ellery, watches her from the porch and warns her gently to leave. Emotional beat: dread deepening into investigation; the past has an address.

chapters.title: What the Archive Kept
chapters.summary: Lena drives to the county records office and finds the parish register torn out—pages cut cleanly from 1811. POV: Lena. A retired librarian mentions the founding families 'made peace' with something that winter. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery curdling as she realizes the erasure was deliberate, communal, and old.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Tom's granddaughter, Wren, secretly plays Lena a cassette her grandmother recorded decades ago: the hymn, sung fully but wrong—the final verse replaced by humming. POV: Wren. That night, Lena hums it back and the mirrors lag two seconds. Emotional beat: loyalty tested—Wren risks family secrets to help a stranger.

chapters.title: Reflections Out of Order
chapters.summary: The reflections begin acting independently: Lena's mirror-self mouths words she isn't saying. Reading lips, she deciphers 'the last verse.' POV: Lena. She barricades the bedroom but hears humming through the walls. Emotional beat: isolation and terror; the haunting now speaks directly to her.

chapters.title: Ellery's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Vicar Ellery invites Lena for tea and admits the church knows: Marguerite was drowned by the founders in 1811, accused falsely, and the hymn was written to bind her spirit. POV: Ellery. He believes singing the final verse maintains the binding and begs Lena to stop digging. Emotional beat: duty versus truth—Ellery is sympathetic, sincere, and wrong.

chapters.title: Twelve Years Ago
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: young Lena, then a student, recorded the full hymn from Marguerite's last living descendant, Ada, who died that same night. POV: Lena (past). Lena fled with the tape and never listened to it. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing—Lena's 'innocence' was complicity; she has carried the answer all along.

chapters.title: The Tape
chapters.summary: In the present, Lena finally plays Ada's tape. Ada's voice teaches the final verse—then the recording continues past where it should end, and something else answers. POV: Lena. The mirrors shatter except one. Emotional beat: devastating revelation; knowledge brings no safety, only obligation.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren reveals the Brackens have served as the hymn's keepers for generations, singing it once yearly at the grave. Her grandmother's death broke the schedule; the lagging began the day Lena arrived. POV: Wren. She asks Lena to leave before the solstice. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth—Wren loves her village and knows it is damned.

chapters.title: The Village That Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Lena confronts the town council; they admit everything calmly, even gratefully—one verse sung once a year is a small price. POV: Lena. Their placid acceptance horrifies her more than the ghost. Emotional beat: moral revulsion; the true monster is institutionalized injustice.

chapters.title: Humming in the Walls
chapters.summary: The haunting escalates: the house hums the hymn continuously, mirrors appear in windows that shouldn't have them, and Lena sees a wet-haired woman standing at the garden gate each midnight. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: siege mentality; Lena stops sleeping, starts writing the verse down obsessively.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Lena attempts to memorize the final verse silently, mouthing the words. Each attempt, the mirror-woman comes closer, and Lena tastes river water. POV: Lena, intercut with Marguerite's fragmented memory-dreams of 1811. Emotional beat: intimate horror—the ghost isn't attacking; she's teaching, and teaching costs.

chapters.title: Ellery's Confession, Part Two
chapters.summary: Ellery breaks: his own brother vanished years ago trying to alter the ritual. He gives Lena the founders' original letter admitting Marguerite's innocence. POV: Ellery. Emotional beat: grief and surrender; duty collapses under truth, and Ellery chooses to help Lena end it.

chapters.title: The Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: The village gathers at the churchyard for the annual singing. Lena attends uninvited, recorder hidden, planning to disrupt the rite. POV: Lena. When the congregation reaches the broken verse, the silence afterward stretches too long—and something below the ground inhales. Emotional beat: dread at maximum; the ritual is failing.

chapters.title: What Rises When the Song Stops
chapters.summary: The binding snaps. Cold floods the churchyard; graves weep water; the congregation flees screaming as Marguerite rises fully, no longer gentle. POV: alternating Lena and Wren. Emotional beat: chaos and consequence—twelve years of denial come due at once.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Alone before the open grave, Lena sings the true final verse aloud—not the binding version, but Marguerite's own words, naming her killers and declaring her innocent. POV: Lena. The ghost stops, listens, and weeps. Emotional beat: courage and catharsis; justice spoken at last, whatever it costs.

chapters.title: The Price of a Voice
chapters.summary: The debt demands a singer. The mirror appears one last time showing Lena's place beneath the stone, and she accepts—until Wren steps forward and begins the verse, and one by one the villagers return and sing with her. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: sacrifice answered by solidarity; love against duty resolved in favor of both.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Rest
chapters.summary: Sung by many voices, the hymn transforms from chain to elegy. Marguerite's spirit bows and dissolves like mist off the river; the water recedes; dawn comes warm. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: release and awe—the horror ends not with banishment but with acknowledgment.

chapters.title: After the Singing
chapters.summary: Weeks later: the mirrors show only the present. The village holds a funeral for Marguerite, carving her name in full, and votes to teach the whole hymn openly. Ellery resigns; Wren becomes the new keeper of a song kept in daylight. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: quiet reckoning; justice outside the law becomes memory inside the community.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Lena publishes her fieldwork complete, final verse included, dedicated to Ada and Marguerite. On her last night in the cottage, she plays the recording once—and hears, faintly beneath it, a single voice humming along, grateful and gone. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure; some songs are finished only when someone dares to sing them twice.
